4.0.s.en: 1. Oppression and the loss of humanity:

4.0.0.en: 1 So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter. 2 Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive. 3 Yea, better is he than both they, which hath not yet been, who hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.

4.0.1.en: The Preacher declares that oppression is the mark of all the works of man [1]; the oppressed appear unable to act, and their cry tears the heart of the Preacher. Solomon was so tender in his feelings that he could not bear the tears of the oppressed, counting the dead more blessed than the living who see injustice prevailing in the world, and the miscarriage, which is not born but dies like a child in its mother's womb, more blessed than all, because it "hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun" [3].

4.0.2.en: The Preacher was not pessimistic in his longing for death; rather he was tender to the utmost, unable to bear the sight of the oppressed, imitating his Lord who says: "Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me" (Song 6:5)... Perhaps the Preacher himself also feared lest he should share in the oppression and fall prey to it.

4.0.3.en: St. Ambrose expresses the feelings of the Preacher, who longed for death rather than see injustice, saying: [The Preacher affirms that one born dead is better than one advanced in age, because he has not seen the evils that have befallen this world. He has not come into that darkness, nor walked in the vanity of the world; therefore he who has not come into this life is more at rest than he who has come into it. Truly, what is the good of man in this life? He lives in darkness and is not satisfied in his desires, and when he is gorged with riches he lacks rest, since he is bound to guard the possessions he has acquired because of his wicked greed. Because he acquired that property by gluttony and covetousness, he sees that it gives him no good. How bitter it is that a man should guard his possessions and be tormented and not profit by their abundance!].

4.0.4.en: If the Preacher praises one who died in his mother's womb so that he might not see injustice, or might not share in men's injustice, covetousness and greed, should we not all the more call blessed the one who dies of his own free will with his crucified Christ, out of love for God and men? As Origen says: [Who is to be praised with more worthiness than he who dies in the full freedom of his will for the sake of his religion (his faith)?!].

4.1.0.en: 4 Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit. 5 The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh. 6 Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.

4.1.1.en: The Preacher criticizes those who rely on idleness and the seeking of ease, either because they feel the injustice around them and are overcome by frustration, asking: What have those who acquired abundant riches gained? Or because, in practicing injustice, they seek to grow rich at the expense of their brethren, and so they seek ease in relaxation in order to reap the fruit of the labor of others. In any case the Preacher asks the believers for a life of moderation, without extremes either toward slackness and idleness or toward exaggeration in seeking wealth and possessions.

4.1.2.en: "Again, I considered all travail, and every right work (success), that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit" [4].

4.1.3.en: What man thinks to be success in his work, when he gathers and hoards, comparing himself with others and envying his neighbor who acquires more than he, is vanity and a seizing of the wind... for it corrupts man's inner nature, driving it to practice injustice and oppression instead of love and mercy. St. Gregory the Wonder-worker says: [It has also become clear to me how dangerous is the envy that afflicts a man toward his neighbor like the sting of an evil spirit, and I have seen that he who falls prey to it, and whose breast is filled with it, can do nothing but eat and tear his own heart! His soul collapses and his body wastes away, for he finds no comfort in the good things of others].

4.1.4.en: St. Basil the Great says: [There is no passion worse or more harmful than envy. It does not harm the neighbor so much as it harms the envious man himself. Envy is a worm that gnaws in the depths of man's heart, and works in it as rust works on iron. It is dejection of soul and grief that befalls a man at the sight of the happiness others enjoy... The worst thing about envy is that it is a sickness that is kept hidden. You see the envious man with lowered gaze and sullen face, constantly complaining of inner torment, which withers his face and wears out his body, so that he grows thin and weak. He is ashamed to say: "I am envious," I feel bitterness and sorrow at the good that another man has obtained, I am tormented by the happiness of my friends, and I cannot bear the success of my peers. I see that the happiness of others is a sword that tears my bowels and pierces me to the heart...

4.1.5.en: The envious man, besides what we have mentioned, loses the right sense and feeling for values... With him virtue becomes vice, and good becomes evil. Thus the brave man is considered by the envious to be rash, the prudent dull, the righteous a criminal, the wise a hypocrite, the generous wasteful and prodigal, and the thrifty miserly. All virtues become vices in the eyes of the envious].

4.2.0.en: "The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh" [5].

4.2.1.en: The idle man, whether fleeing from the injustice of others or intending to benefit from the labor of others without sharing their work, gains nothing. He folds his hands from work, and so loses everything and finds not even what to eat... so he eats his own flesh. This is a figurative expression meaning to die of hunger, or meaning that the idle man enters a state of inner emptiness; instead of thinking of positive work he is confused by many exaggerated thoughts, which destroy his psychological state and rob him of his health, even his bodily health.

4.2.2.en: * There is no need for me to describe to you the gravity of the evil of idleness, when the Apostle commanded plainly: "If any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thess 3:10). For as daily food is necessary for every man, so toil according to his strength is necessary for him. Solomon did not write in vain, in praise of the diligent woman: "[she] eateth not the bread of idleness" (Prov 31:27), as the Apostle also said of himself: "Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day" (2 Thess 3:8), although he had the authority, as a preacher of the Gospel, to live of the Gospel (1 Cor 9:14); indeed the Lord (in His discourse) joined idleness with evil, when He said: "Thou wicked and slothful servant" (Mt 25:26). Moreover, wise Solomon did not only commend the worker as we have mentioned (Prov 31:27) but rebuked the idle man by likening him to the lowest of creatures (the insects), saying: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard" (Prov 6:6). Therefore we must fear lest we too be rebuked on the day of judgment, because He who gave us the ability to work asks of us works that suit this ability, for He said: "To whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more" (Lk 12:48).

4.2.3.en: And since some shrink from work on the pretext of prayers and the chanting of the Psalms, such people must know that for everything there is its own time, as the Preacher said: "To every thing there is a season" (Eccl 3:1).

4.3.0.en: St. Basil the Great "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit" [6].

4.3.1.en: It is better for a man to work so as to enjoy a handful with ease of heart and peace of soul than to venture violently in envy and zeal for the sake of hoarding and abundance of riches, and so actually gain a double yield but with anxiety and disturbance; for in reality he reaps the anxiety that crushes him, that is, he reaps a seizing of the wind. St. Paul says his final word on this: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content... I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Phil 4:11-13).

4.3.2.en: In the Conferences of St. John Cassian, Abba Abraham sees that the words of wise Solomon here explain the superiority of quiet work in the wilderness, with some inner rest and security, over care for serving others while being immersed with them in their material affairs, for he says: [It is better for us to persevere constantly in our purpose, acquiring a moderate gain in the wilderness, where there are no worldly cares or entanglements that scatter the mind, no pride and no vainglory, and where the cares of daily necessities are fewer... This is better than seeking great gain through conversing with others in a most profitable discourse, while we become immersed in the demands of secular life, which is full of daily entanglements. For Solomon says: "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit." In these snares the weak fall... for while they are careless of their own salvation, and while they themselves need the teaching and guidance of others, they are deceived by the wiles of Satan under the cover of bringing others to repentance and guiding them].

4.4.0.en: 7 Then I returned, and I saw vanity under the sun. 8 There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This is also vanity, yea, it is a sore travail. 9 Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. 10 For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up. 11 Again, if two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone? 12 And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

4.4.1.en: The Preacher reveals the folly of the oppressors from many sides. The oppressor, in his love of acquiring and hoarding, envies his neighbor for what he has, and so loses his inner peace... He remains in a state of constant hunger however much wealth he gains [4]. Injustice may drive him to slackness and idleness, that he may unjustly reap the fruits of his neighbor, and while he is in slackness and idleness he finds that he eats his own flesh, and so does not enjoy true rest [5]. Or he may go to another extreme, working without limits in order to acquire manifold wealth, and then he reaps only toil and a seizing of the wind [6]. Finally, his selfishness may drive him into a state of extreme misery when he is cut off from the company of others, sacrificing every friendship and every love of sharing for the sake of hoarding wealth, which the Preacher expressed, saying:

4.4.2.en: "Then I returned, and I saw vanity under the sun. There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches" [7-8].

4.4.3.en: He gives an example: a man isolated in selfishness even from his brothers and his sons, as though he had no brothers and no sons. He gathers much, but he deprives himself, as he deprives those nearest to him, of meeting in the circle of love, and he does not know what will be the end of what he gathers!

4.4.4.en: How bitter I felt while I was in the United States when I learned that a man and his son had resorted to the courts, each claiming ownership of a project in which they had shared and which had brought abundant profit... The love of money destroys even fatherhood and sonship! Can money satisfy the heart of a man who isolates himself from everyone, even from his son?!

4.4.5.en: * One who is left alone in harsh isolation, without brother or son, yet possesses a vast and rich estate, lives in greedy gluttony and refuses to give himself to any good work!

4.4.6.en: The gravest calamity of the man who owns vain wealth (in covetousness) is his lack of a friend to help him and bring gladness to his heart. But those who live together multiply the good wealth that falls into their hands, and their fellowship lessens the pressure of the storms of hateful events. For by day they are distinguished by their strong trust in one another, and by night they are marked by cheerfulness and patience. But he who lives a life of isolation is filled with dread...

4.4.7.en: St. Gregory the Wonder-worker If injustice drives a man to isolation, so that for one reason or another he cannot bear true fellowship, therefore the Preacher urges us to practice a life of fellowship, team work and active, effective friendship, saying:

4.4.8.en: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.

4.4.9.en: For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.

4.5.0.en: But woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up" [9-10].

4.5.1.en: Relying on these words, St. Pachomius made it a rule that no monk should dwell alone in a cell.

4.5.2.en: Working friendship has its effectiveness and is necessary in the life of faith, and as the Jewish proverb in the Talmud says: "Either companionship or death."

4.5.3.en: * I always long to form close relationships with the righteous, and I am often moved to love them. For we read: "Two are better than one... if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" [9].

4.5.4.en: St. Jerome * The lover of the saints is a companion of the angels.

4.5.5.en: * Let your conversation be with those who love God, that your soul may take on the likeness of their purity.

4.5.6.en: St. John Saba Church history tells us of wonderful examples of friendships and the spiritual blessings they brought into the lives of the saints. We mention, for example, the friendship that arose between St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nazianzus, of whom the latter says: [I breathe you in more than I breathe the air, and whether I am present or absent, I live only the time in which you are with me]. He also says: [When we became acquainted and our common desire to study true philosophy became clear, each of us became everything to the other. We had one roof over our house and one table at which we studied, and shared sentiments. Our eyes soared toward one goal, and our affection only grew and became firmer day by day. Bodily passions pass away, but the love that has a bond with God is steadfast because its place is steadfast, and the more its beauties become clear and are revealed, the more it binds together those whom it has joined in the same bond of love].

4.5.7.en: And St. Basil offers us his experience of this friendship, saying:

4.5.8.en: [In life in community a man does not enjoy only his own particular gift, but multiplies it by sharing it with others, and gathers fruit from their gifts as he gathers from his own gift].

4.5.9.en: [But the man who hides in himself the graces and gifts God has granted him, and does not share their benefits with others, is condemned like one who buried his talent].

4.5.10.en: Some of the Fathers see in the Preacher's saying, "Two are better than one," a confirmation of the necessity of a spiritual father who supports the believer lest he deviate according to his own self-will.

4.5.11.en: * Many desire virginity while they are still young and of little understanding; these must be occupied before everything with seeking a suitable guide and teacher for this way, lest in their present ignorance they turn aside from the right way and fall into another road, rugged in its paths, of their own devising. "Two are better than one," so says the wise man, for it is easy for one to be defeated at the hands of the adversary who sets his snares on the road that leads to God; and truly "woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up."

4.5.12.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa On the other hand, it befits each of us to be concerned to raise up his brother in a spirit of meekness and love, as the Preacher says: "If they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" [9].

4.5.13.en: * In practicing the work of the Preacher, set before your eyes that you direct your life well, and that you pray for the foolish that they may gain understanding and know how to cease from evil deeds.

4.5.14.en: St. Gregory the Wonder-worker The Preacher offers us examples to confirm the importance of friendship and spiritual fellowship for edification:

4.5.15.en: The first example: "If two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone?!"

4.5.16.en: He means those who lie together to keep each other warm, travelers in desert regions bitterly cold at night who do not have sufficient coverings; or perhaps he means a good married life, which grants family warmth and satisfaction within the soul in the Lord.

4.6.0.en: The second example: "And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken" [12]. That is, if friendship and partnership with another gives a man strength, so that if one attacks him two stand against him, what then if the fellowship is among three? Cords woven of three strands endure more than those woven of two.

4.6.1.en: What is this threefold cord but the unity of the Church community, in whose midst the Lord Christ dwells according to His promise: "If two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them"? St. Jerome sees that it represents the bond between faith, hope and love, saying: [The words of the Apostle about faith, hope and love are like the threefold cord that is not easily broken. We believe and we hope, and through our faith and our hope we are bound to one another with the bond of love].

4.7.0.en: 13 Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. 14 For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor. 15 I considered all the living which walk under the sun, with the second child that shall stand up in his stead. 16 There is no end of all the people, even of all that have been before them: they also that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and vexation of spirit.

4.7.1.en: Having presented the Preacher's testimony about the vanity of the world, where injustice prevails over mankind and takes the place of justice, and because of which some in folly seek ease at the expense of others, their hearts inflamed with envy and jealousy, while others withdraw into themselves in selfishness instead of working together as a team in a spirit of sharing and love, many also spoil their labor by seeking vainglory and temporal honor at any cost; yet this honor depends on the fluctuations of men and is therefore without security... A prisoner may come out to the throne, and a king may descend to prison.

4.7.2.en: Man's true greatness is not in the multitude of his days, nor in his position or his abilities, but in the wisdom that dwells in him: "Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished" [13]... He is a king of many days with all abilities, but by lacking wisdom he lacks a life of watchfulness.

4.8.0.en: He affirms that conditions do not last; a man may come out of prison to the throne, like Joseph, and a king may be driven from his throne [14]. The first gains the love of men while the second is hated. Perhaps by the one who comes out of prison he meant man himself, for he was born from his mother's womb naked, as one in a prison, only to find himself occupying the throne without struggle or skill or abilities of his own or any personal privilege of his own.

4.8.1.en: The one who comes out of prison to the kingdom points to the men of the New Testament who are freed from the prison of the letter of the Law, and the deposed king is the Jews, who have in their hands the Law and the prophecies and the divine promises but denied faith in the Savior. By the letter the leaders of the Jews lost the kingdom, and by faith the believers became kings and priests (Rev 1:6) in the life of Baptism.

4.9.0.en: When the Jewish leader, literal in worship, loses his spiritual kingship, the people gathered around him leave him to enjoy the work of faith in Christ, the Giver of the kingdom, and the true believers also do not rejoice in him [16].

4.9.1.en: Origen sees that the one who comes out of prison to the kingdom is the martyr who goes forth to the King of kings to enjoy a lasting throne that is not taken from him, for he says: ["Out of prison he cometh to reign." Thus I was persuaded to die for the truth, despising at once what is called death. Bring the fierce beasts, bring the crosses, offer the fires, come, you tormentors. I know that when I die I go out of my body and rest with Christ].

4.9.2.en: Thus, as the Preacher used the testimony of society in the world and the injustice it bears because of the selfishness of some of the rich and those in authority, he calls all to a spirit of love and sharing, far from the seeking of vainglory.
